facts.claim: "Brave Man's Death" is a 5:21 track on the band's 2010 self-titled album. Credits list the writers as J. Roddy Walston & The Business and Billy Gordon.
AllMusic credits Billy Gordon with engineering, mixing, guitar and vocals on the album. It credits Roddy Walston with guitar, piano and vocals.
The album was produced by Kevin Augunas. It was recorded in less than two weeks at Sound City Studios and Fairfax Recordings in Los Angeles, with minimal overdubs.
The band recorded to tape on a roughly 40-year-old machine rather than modern digital equipment. Most of the 10-song album was taped live in the studio.
Walston said nearly every take on the album came from the first three takes. He also said the band tried to play the songs well and record them that way, rather than overproduce.

SPIN named "Brave Man's Death" and "Don't Break the Needle" as album high points, describing them as rollicking boogie with soulful lyrics. Walston said of the record, "We didn't want to use computers."
The song's lyrics tell of a son shamed by his father who wants a "brave man's death."
"Brave Man's Death" was used in the MTV reality series "Caged," along with "Don't Break the Needle" and "Pigs and Pearls."
The band played "Brave Man's Death" on NPR's World Cafe in 2010, along with "Don't Break the Needle" and "Full Growing Man."

The band formed in Cleveland, Tennessee in 2002 and moved to Baltimore in 2004. It self-released Hail Mega Boys in 2007 and signed to Vagrant via Fairfax Recordings in November 2009. The self-titled album was released July 27, 2010.

research.lineage: The band plays piano-driven Southern rock 'n' roll rooted in rollicking soul, blues and gospel, with Tennessee Bible-belt roots and a Baltimore base.

draft:
A father who won't give his son his name, then dies proud the day the boy gets a gun. That's where **Brave Man's Death** starts, and everything after is the son trying to earn back what was held from him at birth. "Said he wouldn't put his name on me" is the wound. The rest of the song is the scar tissue.

What makes it hard to shake is how the narrator keeps telling on himself. The father's pride only arrives with a weapon, and the tear in his eye comes with the line about not thinking "of a better way to die." Love, in this family, is something you get by being hard enough to deserve it. Then comes the spoon the lord puts in his mouth: "It tasted so bitter, but I couldn't spit it out." It's an inheritance he didn't choose and can't refuse, tasting of his mother's money, which he steals once she's buried. Her last note tells him to die like a brave man, so even the tender parent hands down the same creed.

He passes it on. He has a woman with kids, and admits flatly that he never loved them. When she dies she tells him life was worth the pain, and he can't take it in. Late in the song there's a knife, a dead man, blood on his hands, and a heart he holds, then hides, because it's tearing him apart. The cry that follows, "God, I want to die like a man," is bravado and begging at once. The chorus fears dying "in the middle of the night," and the closing borrows the child's bedtime prayer, the one that worries about dying before you wake. Underneath the gasoline and salted fields is a kid afraid of going unseen.

The band plays all this as rollicking boogie, and that clash is the point. A distorted, overdriven guitar riff locks in with a bass that holds the floor. The drums hit a strong backbeat with crashing cymbals, and piano chords fill out the middle in the band's Southern rock 'n' roll way, rooted in blues, soul and gospel out of Tennessee's Bible belt. The lead vocal is raspy and pushed forward, doubled by a second voice in unison and parallel lines, so the creed sounds shouted by a crowd. The groove is mid-tempo and driving, never rushed.

The sound is raw and live because it was made that way. Producer Kevin Augunas cut the album in under two weeks at Sound City and Fairfax Recordings in Los Angeles. The band played mostly live to a tape machine about 40 years old, kept overdubs to a minimum, and took nearly everything from the first three takes. Billy Gordon, who engineered and mixed the record, shares the writing credit with the band.

You end up stomping along to a man who learned love only as a dare, and his fear of dying unseen gets under the swagger before you notice.
